idiom_name: CRTP mixin base with in-class friend operators (Barton-Nackman trick / hidden friends)
implementation_notes: The pattern's home. The operator family lives in a class template parameterised on the derived type, and the operators are defined inline as friend non-template functions taking two Derived operands: each instantiation injects its own concrete overload, which only argument-dependent lookup finds and which outranks any namespace-scope operator template. The family member implements just the primitives (equalTo, operator==, operator<) and inherits EqualityComparable<T> / Comparable<T>; the mixins are opt-in, so a type can be equality-comparable without being ordered. On C++20 and later prefer a defaulted operator<=> for member-wise ordering and keep this form for pre-C++20 targets, for non-relational operator families (arithmetic, swap, stream) and for heterogeneous comparison.
pitfalls: The injected friend is invisible to ordinary and qualified lookup - ::operator==(a, b) does not compile and only ADL finds it - which confuses IDEs, code search and error messages.

A friend defined in the class template is a non-template function that participates in conversions on both operands, so adding the mixin can silently change overload resolution at existing call sites (the std::string/StringRef ambiguity resolved in C++20 is the standard-library example).

Each instantiation injects its own function per operator, so a wide family multiplies code size and template-error text; and because the operators are non-members, private inheritance still exposes them.

variants.name: CRTP mixin base with in-class friend operators (classic)
C++20 defaulted operator<=> (spaceship)
variants.implementation_notes: One defaulted declaration makes the compiler generate the whole relational family - and, for a defaulted operator<=>, operator== as well - with member-wise lexicographic semantics, so relational operator mixins become unnecessary for the common case. Write operator<=> by hand (returning std::strong_ordering, weak_ordering or partial_ordering) when ordering is by key or only partial. This variant cannot express arithmetic operator families, heterogeneous comparison or opt-out from a single derived operator, so the CRTP mixin remains for those.
pitfalls: Defaulted comparison follows member declaration order, so reordering members silently changes the ordering, and adding a member can change the comparison category.

A defaulted operator<=> assumes member-wise semantics: hand-written ordering (a normalised date, a key projection, non-member layout) still needs a custom operator<=> - '= default' is not always the drop-in replacement.

variants.name: Boost.Operators mixin templates (library)
variants.implementation_notes: The library form of the same idea: derive from boost::equality_comparable<T> to get !=, from boost::less_than_comparable<T> to get >, <= and >= from <, from totally_ordered<T> for both, or from addable<T> / subtractable<T> / additive<T> for arithmetic, with two-argument forms (less_than_comparable<T, U>) for heterogeneous comparisons. Choose it when the operator subsets should be named, pre-tested components, or when the codebase already depends on Boost instead of owning a hand-rolled mixin base.
pitfalls: less_than_comparable assumes a total order (use partially_ordered otherwise) and totally_ordered still requires you to write operator==: < alone defines equivalence, not equality (Boost's ordering note).
The requirements are checked only when an operator is used, so a missing primitive surfaces as a deep template error at the call site rather than at the class definition.
